hook: A lady of the Japanese court who wrote what may be the world's first novel.

pages.x: She was born around 973 into a minor branch of the mighty Fujiwara clan in Kyoto, Japan's capital. Her father taught her brother the Chinese classics, but she picked them up faster just by listening. Her father sighed: "If only you were a boy!" Girls were not meant to learn Chinese.
She married an older official and had a daughter, but her husband died after only two years, in 1001. Perhaps to cope with her grief, she began to write a story.

The Tale of Genji follows the loves and sorrows of a handsome, gifted prince, and then the next generation, through 54 chapters and hundreds of characters. Written around 1000 to 1012, it explores what people feel and think so deeply that it is often called the world's first novel.

Her story became so popular that around 1005 she was brought to court as a lady-in-waiting to the young empress Shoshi, whom she taught Chinese poetry in secret. Court ladies passed her chapters around, and the emperor himself listened to them read aloud.

Her diary is a sharp picture of court life: the birth of a prince, drinking parties, jealous rivals. She is scathing about another famous writer, Sei Shonagon, author of The Pillow Book: "dreadfully conceited". People called her Murasaki after the heroine of her own book.
The Tale of Genji is the most celebrated work of Japanese literature, painted on scrolls and screens for a thousand years and still read around the world. Murasaki appears on the 2,000-yen note.
